clinicalPearls: Pulsating headache brought on specifically by and occurring only during or after sustained strenuous exercise
Attacks last from minutes up to a couple of days and are often bilateral
It is more common in hot weather and at high altitude and tends to affect younger adults
On first presentation, subarachnoid haemorrhage and arterial dissection must be excluded
Cardiac cephalalgia, in which exertional headache reflects myocardial ischaemia, is an important mimic in those with vascular risk factors
Many patients respond to indometacin or to a warm-up before exercise
reference.pathophysiology: Primary exercise headache is thought to result from exertion-related venous or arterial distension and transient changes in intracranial pressure, without a structural lesion in the primary form. Sustained physical effort raising intrathoracic and intracranial pressure is the trigger, distinct from the brief Valsalva of cough headache. Because the same exertional stress can precipitate serious secondary events, vascular and cardiac causes must be excluded initially.
additionalInvestigations: Brain imaging and vascular imaging on first presentation to exclude haemorrhage and dissection
Cardiac assessment where vascular risk factors suggest cardiac cephalalgia
History distinguishing sustained exertion from Valsalva triggers
Consideration of RCVS workup if recurrent thunderclap features
redFlags: Neck pain or focal deficit suggesting dissection
Exertional headache relieved by rest in a patient with cardiac risk factors
reference.prognosis: The primary form is benign and frequently self-limiting over months to a few years, often manageable with pre-exercise prophylaxis; prognosis of secondary causes depends on the specific diagnosis.
pitfalls: Attributing a first exertional thunderclap headache to a benign cause without excluding haemorrhage
Missing cardiac cephalalgia in an older patient
Confusing it with primary cough headache
Failing to reconsider the diagnosis if the pattern changes
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Offer indometacin as first-line treatment, either symptomatically or as pre-exercise prophylaxis
Advise a graded warm-up before exertion and moderation of intensity, particularly in heat and at altitude
Exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage and arterial dissection with brain and vascular imaging at first presentation
Exclude cardiac cephalalgia with cardiac assessment in patients with vascular risk factors
Consider alternative prophylaxis such as a beta-blocker if indometacin is unsuitable
Reassure about the benign, usually self-limiting course and refer to neurology if features are atypical
